title: Fibremaxing With Indian Food: Dal and Millets Beat Imported Powders
excerpt: The viral trend urges maximising fibre toward the 25-38 gram daily target most adults miss. Traditional Indian staples — dals, millets, vegetables and guava — already do the job, if intake rises gradually.
body:
• 'Fibremaxing' is a social-media trend built on a real gap: adults need about 25 grams of fibre a day (women) to 38 grams (men), while typical intake is only about 10-15 grams.
  • Traditional Indian food already fits the trend — dals, chickpeas and kidney beans, millets such as ragi, jowar and bajra, vegetables, and fruits such as guava and papaya are all high in fibre.
  • Increase slowly: dietitians advise adding roughly 5 grams a week and drinking enough water; jumping from 10 to 35 grams overnight commonly causes bloating, gas and constipation.
  • For readers: you do not need imported powders — swapping refined flour for whole-wheat or multi-millet rotis and adding one cup of dal or beans a day closes much of the 10-23 gram daily shortfall.

After years of protein dominating diet advice, fibre is having a social-media moment. 'Fibremaxing' — deliberately maximising fibre at every meal — is spreading across Instagram and TikTok through bean bowls, chia puddings, lentil salads and whole-grain plates. Unlike crash diets, the trend does not ask followers to cut food groups or buy expensive products. It asks them to add fibre-rich foods to what they already eat.

The Gap the Trend Is Pointing At

The underlying numbers are unglamorous and real. Adults generally need 25 to 38 grams of fibre a day — about 25 grams for women and 38 grams for men — yet typical consumption is only around 10 to 15 grams, according to guidance summarised in a CDC lifestyle-coach guide drawing on US dietary guidelines. Put in absolute terms, most people are short by roughly 10 to 23 grams a day — the equivalent of skipping a cup of cooked lentils and a piece of fruit, every day.

Fibre comes in two forms. Soluble fibre, found in oats, dal, fruit and isabgol (psyllium), dissolves in water, feeds beneficial gut bacteria and helps moderate blood sugar and cholesterol. Insoluble fibre, found in whole wheat, vegetable skins, bran and seeds, adds bulk and helps prevent constipation. Research cited by dietitians in Mint's coverage — a 2019 Lancet analysis — found people eating 25-29 grams a day had a substantially lower incidence of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer than low-fibre eaters. That is an association at recommended intake levels, not a case for unlimited fibre.

"It asks them to add fibre-rich foods to what they already eat."

Indian Kitchens Are Already Equipped

The Indian-food angle is why the trend travels well in the diaspora. A traditional thali is fibre-dense by design. Pulses and legumes — chickpeas, kidney beans, black chickpeas, green gram and everyday dals such as masoor and moong — supply soluble fibre and protein together. Millets including ragi, jowar and bajra, along with oats and brown rice, raise the fibre content of rotis and rice dishes; replacing refined flour with whole-wheat or multi-millet flour is the simplest single swap. Vegetables such as spinach, bottle gourd, carrots, peas and beans add bulk, and fruits eaten with their skin — guava, papaya, apple and pear — are among the cheapest fibre sources available in both Indian and US grocery stores.

How to Start Without the Backlash

Dietitians quoted in coverage of the trend are consistent on method: go gradually. Add about 5 grams of fibre a week so the digestive system can adjust — Her Zindagi's guidance similarly suggests increases of 4-5 grams every few days — and drink enough water, around 2.5-3 litres a day, because fibre absorbs water and can worsen constipation without it. Rushing produces the side effects that give the trend a bad name: bloating, gas, abdominal discomfort and, at very high intakes, reduced absorption of minerals such as iron and zinc.

A practical day that reaches roughly 30 grams without supplements looks ordinary: oats or a millet-based breakfast, a cup of dal or beans at lunch, a whole fruit as a snack, and vegetables plus whole-wheat rotis at dinner. For diaspora readers, that is not a new diet. It is the home food many grew up with, measured against a target most modern, refined-grain-heavy eating quietly misses.
